title: The first martyrs of Rome (30 June)
hookLine: the unnamed Christians killed under Nero

cards: Rome is burning. For days the fire runs through the city, and when it's out, people want someone to blame. Rumors point at the emperor himself.
So Nero points somewhere else: at a small, strange group the city already distrusts, the Christians. What follows is cruel, and public. And almost none of the people who die have names we know.
The day before, the Church honors Peter and Paul, names written all over the New Testament. Today it turns to the ones nobody wrote down. Today, the first martyrs of Rome.

teach.b: The main account comes not from a Christian but from a Roman historian, Tacitus, who had no sympathy for them and calls their faith a superstition.

He records that Nero shifted the blame for the fire onto them, that a great many were arrested, and that they were put to death with mockery: some dressed in animal skins and torn by dogs, some burned as torches when daylight failed.

Even Tacitus says the crowd began to feel pity, sensing these people were dying not for the public good but for one man's cruelty. Tradition places the deaths of Peter and Paul in Rome under Nero too.
But this day is for everyone else.
Paul had once written to this very church. In the Douay-Rheims he tells them: "your faith is spoken of in the whole world."
Some readers wonder how many of the people Paul greets by name at the end of that letter were among those who died. Nobody knows. That's the point of this feast.
The Greek word behind martyr means a witness. In Acts, Jesus tells his followers, "you shall be witnesses unto me." A martyr is someone whose death becomes their testimony.
These martyrs left none we can read: no last words, no letters, no tombs with names.
The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of the faithful as "so great a cloud of witnesses": a crowd, not a list.

teach.h: SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.
teach.b: The Church's calendar has a day for them anyway. They have no names in our books, and the feast rests on the trust that every one of them is known to God.

how: On 30 June the Church keeps an optional memorial of the First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church, the day after the Solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul; Catholics remember them at Mass and often pray for Christians persecuted today.

games.q: you're compiling the Church's calendar. there are martyrs with well-known names, and a crowd with none. what do you do?
o: only list those whose names survive.
give the nameless crowd a day of its own.
fold them quietly into Peter and Paul's feast.
games.why: the calendar gives them 30 June, the day after Peter and Paul, as a feast of their own.

practice: Think of people who have died for their faith, in any age, whose names never made the news, and of people today who face prison or violence for what they believe, in places you may never see.
You don't need their names; hold them as a crowd. If you pray, commend them to God, who knows each one; if you don't, honor them with a minute of attention.

wordCard.voice: Tacitus, the Roman historian who recorded Nero blaming Christians for the great fire. The first martyrs of Rome, killed and remembered together on 30 June.

orig.note: Greek: a witness — the word behind martyr; plural martyres in Acts 1:8.

carryVoice: Your line: no names, all known. The feast keeps the ones the history books lost. Rest well.
